name: Yusuf Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Milking at five, every day, Christmas included. We've 90 dairy cows at Five Oaks, plus wheat and maize for feed, about 160 hectares. I farm it with my younger brother Hassan, and my father still walks the fields every morning even though he's seventy. My wife Amina does the farm's books and keeps us all fed, and we've two children, Omar and Sara.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a good day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A good day is when the milk's in the tank, the cows are content and we're at the table together at seven. On Fridays I go to prayers in town and see half the farmers in the valley afterwards. My grandfather started this farm with six cows and a borrowed bull, and I'd like Omar to have it with more than that. I've never touched any of this AI business, and I won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it. Lot of noise from people in cities who've never done a day's work outside. I'd say that after Friday prayers to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, relief. I wouldn't have to think about it. The farm carries on the way it's carried on for three generations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Milk, sell, pay the bank, save what's left. I'd keep putting money aside for Omar to take over one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there any of your neighbours who'd be disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young Dawson boy, he's mad for gadgets. He's got a drone counting his sheep. A drone can count sheep, but it's never had to carry a lamb through snow. He'll learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the milk price, would anything change there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dairy company sets the price and we take it, that's always been the way. If they use computers to squeeze us harder, that's their game. We've survived worse.

S0.say: I'd say I knew it, and that it was a lot of noise from city people who've never worked outside. I'd say that after Friday prayers to anyone listening.
S0.think: Privately I'd feel relief that I don't have to think about it. The farm would carry on as it has for three generations.
S0.do: Carries on milking, selling and paying the bank, and saves what's left. Keeps putting money aside so his son Omar can take over the farm one day.
S0.quote: A drone can count sheep, but it's never had to carry a lamb through snow.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf's sense of himself is tied to three generations on the farm and passing it to his son. He dismisses AI as city noise. His jab at a young neighbour's drone shows pride in hands-on knowledge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the market sort it out. Good farmers will keep farming. I don't want the government stepping in with grants for robots, they always get these things wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit worried. The big dairies would buy robot milkers and drive the price down, and I don't want robots in my parlour. But a cow still needs a herdsman, and we've the land paid for, most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd put more aside, maybe another few hundred a month. If the dairy company insisted on some computer system, I'd let Hassan deal with it, he's more patient than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the sky before rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want government grants. What if your neighbours took them and got ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then they'd be farming on taxpayers' money, and I'd be farming on mine. I'd rather be a poorer farmer who owns his own cows than a richer one who owes the government for his robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father make of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh. He saw the first milking machines come in and said the same things I'm saying now. He'd say farming always changes and the family carries on.

S1.say: I'd say let the market sort it out, because good farmers will keep farming. I don't want government grants for robots; they always get these things wrong.
S1.think: Privately I'd be a bit worried that big dairies with robot milkers would drive the price down. But a cow still needs a herdsman and most of our land is paid for.
S1.do: Carries on as he is and saves a few hundred more each month. Leaves any computer system the dairy company demands to his brother Hassan.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like the sky before rain.
S1.quote: I'd rather be a poorer farmer who owns his own cows than a richer one who owes the government for his robots.
S1.fieldNote: Yusuf rejects government help on principle, preferring to own his cows outright even if poorer. He'd hand any new system to his brother rather than learn it. His father's memory of the first milking machines gives him a sense that families outlast change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has been forced on ordinary people by a handful of rich men in tech and politicians who don't know one end of a cow from the other. I wouldn't hold back. I'd say it at the mosque, at the market, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it would ruin us. Not overnight, we've land and savings, but the big robot dairies would make milk so cheap we couldn't sell ours at a living price. Two years isn't time to do anything, and I don't know what I'd do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold onto the cash and stop anything that isn't needed, Amina and I would sit down that week. I'd lean on family, my brother and my father, and we'd decide together, the way we always have. I wouldn't buy a robot. I'd rather sell the cows and rent out the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Angry, more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather sell the cows. Is that really what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. It would break my father's heart. I'd keep ten cows in the old shed just so Omar knows what milking smells like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think would help your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family and the community, not the government. The mosque runs a fund for people in hard times. We'd be giving to it, not taking from it, God willing.

S2.say: I'd say this has been forced on ordinary people by rich tech men and politicians who don't know one end of a cow from the other. I'd say it at the mosque, at the market, everywhere.
S2.think: Privately I think it would ruin us over time, because robot dairies would make milk too cheap to sell at a living price. Two years isn't enough to do anything, and I don't know what I'd do anyway.
S2.do: Holds onto cash and cuts anything that isn't needed after sitting down with Amina that week. Decides the farm's future together with his brother and father, and would sooner sell the cows and rent out the land than buy a robot.
S2.quote: I'd keep ten cows in the old shed just so Omar knows what milking smells like.
S2.fieldNote: Yusuf's alarm comes out as anger at tech elites and politicians. He would turn to family and his faith community rather than the state, and is proud to be a giver to the mosque's fund. His plan to keep ten cows for his son shows the farm is more about identity than income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for families to sort themselves out without waiting for government. I'd say farmers should stick together and help each other through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is a bit better. Omar would be eighteen, so we'd have to talk properly about the farm. I'd still not want robots in my parlour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming and saving, and I'd pay off the last of the land loan within three years. I'd talk to Omar, honestly, about whether he still wants the farm, or wants to study first. Hassan and I would look at turning some milk into cheese or yogurt to sell ourselves, because people might still pay for something made by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More about Omar than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The cheese is a change. Isn't that new for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother made cheese in the back kitchen when I was a boy. So it's not new, it's old. If I have to change, I'd rather go backwards to my mother's kitchen than forwards to a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Omar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the farm is his if he wants it, robot or no robot. But I'd want him to learn a trade too, a proper apprenticeship, so he's got something in his hands.

S3.say: I'd say five years is long enough for families to sort themselves out without waiting for government. I'd say farmers should stick together and help each other through it.
S3.think: Privately five years is a bit better, since Omar would be eighteen and we'd have to talk properly about the farm. I still wouldn't want robots in my parlour.
S3.do: Keeps farming and saving and pays off the last of the land loan within three years. Talks honestly with Omar about the farm and an apprenticeship, and looks with Hassan at making cheese or yogurt to sell directly.
S3.feel: Anxious, more for his son than for himself.
S3.quote: If I have to change, I'd rather go backwards to my mother's kitchen than forwards to a robot.
S3.fieldNote: Yusuf frames the cheese idea as going backwards to his mother's kitchen rather than forwards to robots, which lets him change without feeling he's giving in. His worry centres on Omar. He wants his son to take an apprenticeship, in line with his views on work over handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and a good farmer plans for the long term anyway. I'd say we don't need the government telling us how to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's still the end of the farm as I know it, just slower. I'd be 53 and still farming. The question is whether there's anything left for Omar, and I can't answer that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd farm on, the way I do now, and keep saving. I'd get the cheese going in the first couple of years, so it's established before the robots arrive. I'd want Omar to do his apprenticeship and decide for himself. I'd let Hassan look into robots, if he wants, but not in my lifetime in that parlour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but slow. Like watching water rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say not in your lifetime. Even with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even then. I know it's stubborn. Ten years just gives me longer to watch it come up the lane. My father was stubborn too, and the farm's still here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Omar asked me to. If he came home and said, Dad, I want to farm, but with the machines. Then I'd listen. Family first.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and a good farmer plans long-term anyway. I'd say we don't need the government telling us how to do it.
S4.think: Privately it's still the end of the farm as I know it, only slower. The question is whether anything will be left for Omar, and I can't answer it.
S4.do: Farms on as now and keeps saving, getting the cheese business established in the first couple of years. Encourages Omar to do an apprenticeship and decide for himself, and leaves robots to his brother Hassan.
S4.feel: Anxious, but slowly, like watching water rise.
S4.quote: Ten years just gives me longer to watch it come up the lane.
S4.fieldNote: More time doesn't calm Yusuf, because for him the end point is the loss of a family way of life. He knows he's stubborn and says so. The only thing that would change his mind is his son asking, which shows family outranks everything else.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time to do anything properly. What would help is a fair milk price, that the dairy companies can't just drop when the robot farms come in, and keeping the land in families, not sold off to big companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Some things you can't put on a machine. Working with animals, thanking God for a good harvest. People will need that more, not less.

headlineQuote: My grandfather started this farm with six cows and a borrowed bull, and I'd like Omar to have it with more than that.
portrait: Yusuf Rossi is 43 and farms Five Oaks, a 90-cow dairy with wheat and maize, alongside his brother and his seventy-year-old father, three generations on the same land. He's never used AI and won't have robots in his milking parlour. He believes in markets, family and faith over government help, and blames tech elites and politicians for fast change. He's calm when AI fizzles, alarmed and angry at AGI in two years, and still anxious with ten years, because for him the end point means losing the farm he wants to hand to his son Omar.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because there'd be no time to do anything properly.
whatWouldHelp: A fair milk price the dairy companies can't drop when robot farms arrive, and keeping land in families rather than sold to big companies.
